question: Under Ind AS 115, when does a real estate developer recognise revenue for a residential flat?
before: Revenue recognised when control transfers -- at handover/possession for most Indian residential real estate. Not at booking, construction milestone, or financing arrangement. Why real estate revenue is lumpy.
after:
Concept: Ind AS 115 (Revenue from Contracts with Customers) requires an entity to recognise revenue when it transfers control of a promised good or service to a customer. Control means the customer has the ability to direct the use of and obtain substantially all benefits from the asset.

Why this is correct: Under Ind AS 115, for a residential flat sale, the developer recognises revenue at the point of possession or handover, when legal and physical control of the property passes to the buyer. At that moment, the customer obtains the right to occupy, use, and benefit from the flat, satisfying the revenue recognition criterion.

Why the others are wrong: Option A (When customer books and pays token) represents initial commitment and a partial payment, but control has not yet transferred — the developer still retains possession and the right to complete construction. Option B (When construction reaches 50%) is an arbitrary construction milestone and does not reflect the transfer of control; the flat remains under developer control and the buyer cannot occupy it. Option D (When customer takes home loan) is purely a financing event with no connection to the transfer of asset control and does not trigger revenue recognition under Ind AS 115.

Intuition: Real estate revenue recognition under Ind AS 115 is tied to the practical handover moment because that is when the customer's right to the asset becomes complete and enforceable. This creates a lag between booking (which appears in future commitments) and reported revenue, making real estate company earnings lumpy and concentrated in quarters with high possession volumes — a critical pattern for equity analysts to track when modelling cash flow stability and recognising period-to-period volatility.
